findings.family: Prior work on aircraft, rotorcraft, UAM and drone noise propagation in urban environments with buildings: models, measured and simulated dB effects, and validation

models.name: Image-source (specular) method for canonical corner and street-canyon geometries, used as a reference for urban ray codes (ONERA, Malbéqui; CSTB Mithra-SOUND)
models.physics_captured: Coherent sum of the direct field and the image sources from perfectly reflecting ground and facades. A canyon of two parallel infinite walls plus the ground uses ns = 2(nr+1) image sources for reflection order nr. Narrowband interference is computed, then averaged into octave bands from 63 Hz to 8 kHz. The ray code being tested (Mithra) adds finite buildings and edge diffraction.
models.limitations: The reference assumes infinite, perfectly rigid planes, with no finite-height roof edges, no absorption and no scattering. The source is stationary. There is no atmosphere (wind or temperature gradients around buildings), which the author names as the next step, along with moving sources and buildings lower than the source. Ray theory is stated to fail below a few tens of Hz. The canyon test that gave +14 dB put the source at only 10 m, inside the canyon, which is not the elevated-helicopter case. For a source at 30 m and 700 m away above a corner, the octave-band spectrum keeps a single destructive dip, near 250 Hz to 1 kHz depending on geometry.
models.cost: Analytic. For a canyon it costs O(nr) complex exponentials per frequency per receiver, so microseconds per frequency at order 10-50. The paper reports no timings for Mithra.
models.niceops_fit: This is the cheapest physically meaningful urban add-on, and it is exactly a per-receiver transfer function. For a receiver in a canyon of width W and height H, the image lattice is fixed. Each image is a mirrored observer, so reciprocity gives the urban term as a sum over image observers at the same source state, each with its own sphere lookup direction and range. Rotor directivity is then applied per image, which a single precomputed |H(f)| cannot do. With nr ~ 5-10 and an elevated source, an image is visible only if its path passes through the canyon opening, so most are culled geometrically. Cost scales with the number of visible images times the spectral evaluation (~1 us), so 10-100x the current spectral cost per pair at canyon receivers only. That is feasible for scattered microphone sets but heavy for a 120x120 grid times 1e8. Band-averaged incoherent image sums are much cheaper and are what the octave-band results suggest is adequate above ~250 Hz. It can also serve as NICEOPS's own verification case, exactly as ONERA used it.

references.citation: Malbéqui, P. (2023). Assessment of sound propagation for the urban air mobility. Forum Acusticum 2023, Turin, pp. 1011-1014.
references.supports_claim: Image-source references for corner and canyon, 63 Hz-8 kHz octave bands, source at high altitude. Ray tracing (Mithra) agrees well with the reference. About +8 dB vs free field near a corner. In the canyon, +4 dB when source and receiver share the plane x = 0 and up to +14 dB when they are 100 m apart along it, with the source 10 m high. Earlier Mithra run at 500 ft above the Airbus Helicopters Marignane site shows complex spectra near walls.

models.frequency_range_and_scale: 63 Hz-8 kHz in octave bands. Neighbourhood scale (canyon d = 30 m, buildings up to 300 m), with the source up to 700 m away.
models.elevated_moving_source_suitability: The canonical cases include a source at 30 m altitude 700 m away. Moving sources and buildings lower than the source are explicitly left open. Elevation angle sets which images pass through the canyon opening, which a reciprocity lattice captures naturally.

models.name: Engineering urban ray path-finding with standardised attenuation terms (CNOSSOS-EU or ISO 9613-2): NLR's AAM propagation model, CadnaA (Feng and Kang, UCL) and SoundPLAN-style vertiport studies
models.physics_captured: Path search for direct, specularly reflected and edge-diffracted paths (NLR: up to 3 levels deep, buildings as 2.5D extruded outlines). Per-path levels from CNOSSOS-EU or ISO 9613-2: geometric spreading, source directivity (hemisphere), atmospheric absorption, facade reflection loss and diffraction attenuation. Incoherent energy sum per band.
models.limitations: Diffraction is the weak link. Against measurements in NLR Drone DigiCity (24 shipping containers), NLR's model matched reflection-only paths very well in trend and level over 160 Hz-6.3 kHz, but underpredicted by 10-15 dB at a microphone reached mainly by diffraction, with background noise ruled out as the cause. The attenuation terms were built for road and rail sources near the ground and were never calibrated for steep overhead incidence. Feng and Kang find weak frequency dependence of urban attenuation (mostly < 1 dB/octave) and attribute part of it to the ray method's poor low-frequency diffraction. Ground and refraction are treated empirically.
models.cost: Commercial tools such as CadnaA run city districts of 2 km x 2 km with 3D buildings, at minutes to hours per scenario depending on reflection order and search radius (Feng and Kang used a 2000 m radius and a reflection loss of 1 dB). Per path it is a few log and sqrt operations. The path search dominates and depends only on geometry, so it can be precomputed.
models.niceops_fit: The architecture is useful but the attenuation formulas are not. The path topology (which facades and edges link a receiver to a cone of source directions) is purely geometric and can be precomputed per receiver, in line with the roadmap's reciprocity tables. NICEOPS would then supply its own per-band physics (absorption, Weyl-van der Pol ground per reflected leg, a proper edge-diffraction coefficient) instead of the CNOSSOS terms. The NLR result is a strong warning against adopting CNOSSOS diffraction for overhead rotorcraft. Its DigiCity database, an omnidirectional source at 100-400 Hz tones plus broadband and an M600 drone flying at 8.5 and 20 m, is an immediate validation set for any NICEOPS urban module.

references.citation: Knepper, K., Admiraal, P., Lammers, K. (2025). Experimental database for AAM noise assessment in urban environment. 51st European Rotorcraft Forum, Venice.
references.supports_claim: 22-microphone campaign (1.2 m tripods) in NLR Drone DigiCity, with an omni source and a DJI M600 at 8.5 and 20 m. A CNOSSOS-EU ray model with reflections and diffractions up to 3 levels agrees very well on reflection-dominated paths but underpredicts diffraction-dominated paths by 10-15 dB.

references.citation: Feng, T., Kang, J. (2026). Low-altitude aircraft will reshape noise exposure across global cities. arXiv:2609.29763.
references.supports_claim: CadnaA with ISO 9613 and 3D buildings in ten 2x2 km districts, 100 m level flyover. Previously quiet semi-enclosed courtyards rise by more than 20 dB(A). Facade and storey exposure depends on whether the route is visible from that point. Urban attenuation shows weak frequency slope (< 1 dB/octave).

models.frequency_range_and_scale: Octave or third-octave bands, ~100 Hz-8 kHz. Neighbourhood to district scale.
models.elevated_moving_source_suitability: Handles elevated line or point sources in a time-averaged way. Movement enters only through per-position or per-segment summation. Diffraction for steep incidence is unreliable.

models.name: Gaussian beam tracing (GBT) through 3D urban geometry and CFD wind fields (Yunus, Casalino, Avallone, Ragni, TU Delft; Bian, Tan, Zhong, Zhang, HKUST, EARC code)
models.physics_captured: Beams are launched from a noise sphere around the vehicle and traced through an inhomogeneous, anisotropic (moving) atmosphere using CFD wind over the buildings. They undergo multiple specular reflections from 3D terrain and building surfaces. The field at a receiver is a weighted sum of the beams passing nearby, with no eigenray search. A semi-empirical correction handles truncation error for receivers on solid boundaries. Complex source directivity on a sphere carries the ray-sphere intersection shift under refraction. HKUST adds ground impedance and moving-source virtual flights.
models.limitations: No diffracted field behind buildings in the Delft implementation, so the 20-35 dB shadow-zone levels are not physical at low frequency. Building dimensions were chosen at 1.75 wavelengths of the first BPF to avoid diffraction. Without the semi-empirical correction, beam summation on surfaces errs by more than 40 dB. With it, the maximum difference from FEM drops below 8 dB. Accuracy is only as good as the sphere's angular resolution. Validated against FEM only at low frequencies (~100-200 Hz) with three building blocks.
models.cost: Vertiport case (Xeon Gold 6140, 36 cores): GBT 55.7 s against 3.7 s for a straight ray with a single ground image (15x), 46.6 s on flat terrain, 122.5 s with wind. 17x faster than an FEM solve of the convected wave equation at 200 Hz.
models.niceops_fit: This is the closest analogue to NICEOPS: the same sphere-based source paradigm, a footprint output, and Casalino's toolchain. The beam-sum-at-receiver formulation avoids eigenray solves and amortises one beam fan per source position over all receivers, which is the reverse of NICEOPS's per-pair evaluation. For a trajectory of ~6500 states that means ~6500 beam fans, at tens of seconds each in their implementation, so far too slow directly. A per-receiver reverse beam fan (reciprocity), tabulated over source direction and range and then contracted with the sphere per state, gives the roadmap's urban reciprocity table. Its documented weaknesses (no diffraction, surface truncation) mark what NICEOPS would need to add, such as UTD or Biot-Tolstoy edge terms. For inverse use (de-propagation), beams to a fixed microphone are exactly the reciprocal table needed.

references.citation: Yunus, F., Casalino, D., Avallone, F., Ragni, D. (2023). Efficient prediction of urban air mobility noise in a vertiport environment. Aerospace Science and Technology 139, 108410.
references.supports_claim: Building blocks raise ground levels by 0-5 dB in illuminated zones through multiple reflections and create shadow zones, with shielding increasing with frequency. BPF1 vs BPF2 directivity changes the footprint by up to 40 dB. Wind changes lobes, with > 30 dB in a single third-octave band. GBT reduces error vs straight rays by 5 dB (illuminated) and 35 dB (terrain shadow). Run times 55.7 s vs 3.7 s, and 122.5 s with wind. GBT omits diffraction behind buildings.

references.citation: Yunus, F. et al. (2023). Efficient prediction of airborne noise propagation in a non-turbulent urban environment using Gaussian beam tracing method. J. Acoust. Soc. Am. 153(4), 2362-2375.
references.supports_claim: GBT with multiple 3D reflections and wind refraction, validated against FEM of the convected wave equation for three building blocks. Truncation error > 40 dB without the semi-empirical correction and < 8 dB with it. 17x faster than FEM at 200 Hz. Wind weakens diffraction patterns and causes strong refraction above rooftops.

references.citation: Yunus, F. (2023). Methodologies and algorithms for sound propagation in complex environments with application to urban air mobility: a ray acoustics approach. PhD dissertation, TU Delft.
references.supports_claim: Consolidates the GBT work. Helicopter hovering over a mountain with CFD wind: up to 15 dB variation in the illuminated zone from directivity, and upward refraction at the shadow boundary. The frequency-domain source model is ~430x faster than time-domain.

references.citation: Bian, H., Tan, Q., Zhong, S., Zhang, X. (2021). Assessment of UAM and drone noise impact on the environment based on virtual flights. Aerospace Science and Technology 118, 106996 (reprint 125, 107547).
references.supports_claim: GBT solver (EARC) with generic multi-rotor directivity, surface impedance and flight-path effects. Examples of noise impact on a building and a realistic urban environment (dB values not seen in the abstract).

models.frequency_range_and_scale: Validated around 100-200 Hz against FEM and applied to BPF harmonics (~150-300 Hz) and broadband. Vertiport neighbourhood to several-km terrain.
models.elevated_moving_source_suitability: Designed for elevated rotorcraft and eVTOL sources on a noise sphere. HKUST ran moving virtual flights and Delft ran hover. Moving sources are handled quasi-statically, one source position at a time.

models.name: Ray tracing through frozen instantaneous turbulent velocity snapshots from LES or LBM of building wakes (Goyal, de Prenter, Casalino, Ragni, TU Delft)
models.physics_captured: Turbulence-induced level variability (Leq, L10-L90, transient fluctuations) behind a building, from rays traced through a sequence of frozen velocity snapshots. Validated against a time-resolved lattice-Boltzmann VLES that resolves the acoustics directly, with a 100 Hz vertical dipole as a stand-in for AAM tones.
models.limitations: Single 100 Hz tone and one isolated building. The frozen-flow assumption needs velocity decorrelation times (1-2 s) much longer than the acoustic travel time, a ratio above 5 in most of the domain. Signal correlation with LB-VLES varies (r = 0.66 upstream, 0.00 in the acoustic near field, -0.40 where interference patterns shift). Errors are largest near the source and the ground.
models.cost: The reference LB-VLES costs ~2400 CPU-hours for 1000 s of physical time, and 1634 CPU-hours per second at the finest resolution. The ray-tracing part is cheap, and the flow dataset is reusable across sources, frequencies and trajectories.
models.niceops_fit: This is not a deterministic footprint model. What it gives NICEOPS is a magnitude: building-wake turbulence causes ≥ 3 dB level fluctuations, comparable to source variability (~5 dB under gusts). That bounds how precisely a deterministic canyon model can or should resolve interference minima. It argues for partial coherence, through band averaging or a coherence-loss factor, in any urban image or ray sum, in the same spirit as the existing PE turbulence phase screens.

references.citation: Goyal, J., de Prenter, F., Casalino, D., Ragni, D. (2026). Turbulence-induced noise variability from ray tracing with instantaneous velocity snapshots. JASA Express Letters 6(3), 032801.
references.supports_claim: Frozen-snapshot ray tracing reproduces LB-VLES L10-L90 fields and Leq trends. Decorrelation times 1-2 s. LB-VLES cost of ~2400 CPU-h per 1000 s. Source variability up to ~5 dB, of the same order as propagation variability.

references.citation: Goyal, J., de Prenter, F., Ragni, D., Casalino, D. (2026). Impact of building wake turbulence on the noise footprint of a dipole source. J. Acoust. Soc. Am. 159, 1304-1315.
references.supports_claim: Time-resolved LB-VLES of an AAM-like tonal source near an isolated building. Wake turbulence makes received levels fluctuate by more than 3 dB at some locations.

models.frequency_range_and_scale: 100 Hz tone. Single-building scale (a few building heights).
models.elevated_moving_source_suitability: The source sits at or near building height. The method is reusable for any source position in the same flow, so trajectories are possible in principle.

models.name: Wave-based urban solvers (FDTD, ARD, 2D Euler, PSTD, LBM): Albert and Liu (CRREL) 2D FDTD; Raghuvanshi, Mehra, Chandak, Manocha, Wilson, Albert 3D ARD; Dragna, Emmanuelli, Ollivier, Blanc-Benon sonic boom in canyons; Hornikx PSTD courtyards; Casalino LBM
models.physics_captured: Full diffraction, multiple reflection, canyon resonance and over-rooftop propagation. FDTD and Euler solvers can include moving, turbulent media (Wilson's ERDC/CRREL FDTD with turbulent wind and temperature fields). The sonic boom canyon work resolves resonant canyon modes that prolong ground signals.
models.limitations: The bandwidth ceiling is severe. 3D ARD reached ~450 Hz, 2D FDTD and Euler cannot capture rooftop paths properly (3D agrees better with measurement where rooftop propagation matters), and PSTD courtyard work went up to 500 Hz. Domain size for a source at 30-1500 m altitude is prohibitive at kHz frequencies.
models.cost: ARD: a few minutes on a desktop for ~450 Hz in a training-village domain, about 100x faster than FDTD at similar accuracy. LB-VLES: thousands of CPU-hours. FDTD and PSTD at kHz over city blocks: impractical.
models.niceops_fit: Not usable in the per-pair loop. They play the role the Crank-Nicolson PE plays now: an offline reference for a few canonical canyon and courtyard geometries, and a source of per-receiver low-frequency transfer functions, below ~500 Hz where ray methods fail and rotor BPF harmonics live. A hybrid is natural: wave-based below ~300-500 Hz, image or beam methods above, matched in a crossover band, tabulated per receiver over source direction by reciprocity.

references.citation: Albert, D. G., Liu, L. (2010). The effect of buildings on acoustic pulse propagation in an urban environment. J. Acoust. Soc. Am. 127(3), 1335-1346.
references.supports_claim: Explosive-source measurements in a full-scale army training village (15 concrete buildings, 150 x 150 m) compared with 2D FDTD. Diffraction acts as a low-pass filter, greatly reducing shadow-zone peak pressure. Canyon reflections and corner diffraction are documented.

references.citation: Albert, D. G., Liu, L. (2003). Sound propagation in an urban environment. I: Preliminary analysis of measurements.
references.supports_claim: Earlier report on the same artificial-village data. Venue not confirmed.

references.citation: Raghuvanshi, N. (or Mehra, R.), Chandak, A., Manocha, D., Wilson, D. K., Albert, D. G., et al. (2014). Acoustic pulse propagation in an urban environment using a three-dimensional numerical simulation. J. Acoust. Soc. Am. 135, 3231-3242.
references.supports_claim: 3D ARD reaches ~450 Hz usable bandwidth in minutes on a desktop and agrees with measurement better than 2D, especially for over-rooftop propagation.

references.citation: Dragna, D., Emmanuelli, A., Ollivier, S., Blanc-Benon, P. (2022). Sonic boom reflection over an isolated building and multiple buildings. J. Acoust. Soc. Am. (with companion papers on ten realistic urban geometries).
references.supports_claim: 2D Euler simulations. Ground waveforms are multiple arrivals from facade reflections and corner diffraction, plus low-frequency canyon resonances that prolong signals without raising loudness. In compact canyons (high aspect ratio) levels vary strongly from canyon to canyon, and wider streets reduce the influence of the buildings.

references.citation: Hornikx, M., Forssén, J. (2011). Modelling of sound propagation to three-dimensional urban courtyards using the extended Fourier PSTD method. Applied Acoustics.
references.supports_claim: Wave-based courtyard propagation up to 500 Hz (road traffic). 2D overpredicts distant-source contributions, and a facade opening can raise courtyard levels by up to 10 dB(A) relative to over-roof paths.

references.citation: Wilson, D. K., Pettit, C. L., Ostashev, V. E. (2015). Sound propagation in the atmospheric boundary layer. Acoustics Today, Spring 2015.
references.supports_claim: Overview: FDTD handles reflections from buildings and trees and moving turbulent atmospheres, at high computational cost.

models.frequency_range_and_scale: Practical ceiling ~450-500 Hz in 3D at city-block scale. Higher in 2D.
models.elevated_moving_source_suitability: Sonic boom work shows incident waves from aloft handled well in 2D. Elevated moving rotorcraft over 3D blocks at kHz is out of reach. Reciprocity (source at the receiver) makes a single solve serve all source positions.

models.name: Statistical multipath and fading models for urban propagation (Wilson, Bey-Hernandez, Ostashev, ERDC/CRREL)
models.physics_captured: Random building layouts with varying size and density. Ray tracing (checked against FDTD) gives extinction of the coherent field and coherence that decay exponentially with distance, like turbulent scattering. The decay rate rises with building number and size and is nearly frequency independent. Level distributions are compared with radio fading models (Rayleigh, Rice).
models.limitations: Statistical, not site-specific. Developed for ground-level sources and sensors (battlefield acoustics), not overhead sources. The ray tracing omits diffraction.
models.cost: Closed-form statistics once fitted, so negligible per evaluation.
models.niceops_fit: Gives a cheap way to turn deterministic image or beam sums into expected levels with uncertainty bands. For example, treat multipath beyond a few orders as an incoherent diffuse contribution with exponential extinction, or assign SEL confidence intervals per receiver. It is also relevant to inverse use: urban multipath decorrelates the signal, which limits array-based de-propagation.

references.citation: Wilson, D. K., Bey-Hernandez, R., Ostashev, V. E. (2006). Statistical models for fading and coherence of sound in urban environments. J. Acoust. Soc. Am. (abstract/proceedings).
references.supports_claim: Extinction and coherence decay exponentially with distance, at rates set by building number and size, nearly independent of frequency. Ray tracing checked against FDTD.

models.frequency_range_and_scale: Broadband. Ranges of hundreds of metres in built-up areas.
models.elevated_moving_source_suitability: Not developed for elevated sources. Steep incidence into canyons reduces the number of scattering interactions, so the extinction rates would need re-derivation.

models.name: Empirical, scale-model and field data on helicopter, aircraft and drone noise near buildings (Heli-STAR S-76 rooftop tests; Polimi elevated-helipad scale model; TU Delft/AMS field lab near Schiphol; facade-microphone corrections)
models.physics_captured: Measured reflection interference near facades, shielding behind buildings, dependence on observer height, and building shielding of overhead aircraft noise as a function of aircraft orientation, line of sight and facade shape. Also the facade-reflection corrections needed to interpret microphones near walls.
models.limitations: Mostly single sites or scale models with fixed-point (quasi-static) source positions. Scale models miss atmospheric effects: scale vs in-situ differences reach 4.2 dB(A) (σ 2.6) at some microphones. Facade corrections derived with loudspeakers disagree with aircraft overflights by several dB.
models.cost: No simulation cost. The value is as validation data.
models.niceops_fit: These are the validation targets and the error budget. They set the magnitudes an urban module must reproduce: about +3 dB at a reflecting facade (+6 dB flush), 5-15 dB(A) courtyard shielding, and 20-35 dB shielding behind a building at high frequency. They are directly relevant to NICEOPS's flight-test use: microphones near structures pick up reflections of up to 20 dB peak-to-trough in the spectrum at 5 cm from a wall (scale). Such data must be corrected or excluded before de-propagation into source spheres. The existing plate and flush-microphone handling is the analogue for ground boards. A facade receiver type with an image source in the wall is the cheap extension.

references.citation: Gibertini, G., Rezzonico, S., Rossetti, M., Zanotti, A. (2023). Experimental investigation of helicopter noise while approaching an elevated helipad. Aerospace 10(8), 701.
references.supports_claim: Anechoic scale test with a two-blade rotor approaching a reflective prism building, recorded by a surface microphone on the floor. Front of the building reaches about 60 dBA (full-scale equivalent) while most of the rear stays near 25 dBA. Direct-reflected interference swings ~20 dB at 5 cm from the wall and ~10 dB further away, negligible at a distance equal to the building height. Shielding grows with frequency, and wavelengths of 2-3x the building height diffract around it. Also an ERF 2021 paper, 'Helicopter noise in urban flight'.

references.citation: Ahuja, K., Funk, R., Hsu, J., Heiges, M., Stancil, C. (1997). Operation Heli-STAR: Effects of buildings on helicopter noise. DOT/FAA/ND-97/13, Vol. 5.
references.supports_claim: Full-scale S-76 approaches to a rooftop with ~100 microphones near buildings. Shielding and reflection depend clearly on observer height (as summarised by Gibertini et al.; full text not retrieved).

references.citation: Wuite, G., Lugten, M., Tenpierik, M. (2023). Determining causes of variance in ground-level aircraft noise: combining in-situ noise and weather measurements with spatial aircraft data. Forum Acusticum 2023.
references.supports_claim: Full-scale container courtyard field lab near Schiphol. Courtyard shielding is 9.5 dB(A) for line-of-sight flight points and 5.8 dB(A) for non-line-of-sight, with LAeq density peaks at 13 and 5 dB(A). Aircraft orientation explains most variance (R² = 0.58). Earlier work found up to 14.6 dB(A) between exposed and shielded sides.

references.citation: Lugten, M., Wuite, G., Peng, Z., Kim, K., Tenpierik, M. (2023). A scale model approach to simulate aircraft noise in street canyons: a comparison between in-situ and laboratory measurements. Forum Acusticum 2023.
references.supports_claim: 1:50 scale model vs field lab, with microphones 0.2 m from facades at 1.5 and 3.9 m height. Relative-difference agreement is 4.2 dB(A) (σ 2.6), 1.9 dB(A) (σ 1.9) and 0.5 dB(A) (σ 1.9) depending on microphone pair and courtyard. Overhead incidence limits edge shielding, and refraction and cloud cover add variance in situ.

references.citation: Sharp, B., Cox, J. E., Zheng, Z. C. (2018). Investigation of ASTM E966 adjustment factors. FAA report DOT/FAA/TC-18/15.
references.supports_claim: Facade adjustment should be 6 dB for a flush microphone (not 5) and 3.5 dB near the facade (not 2). The loudspeaker method gives several dB lower noise-level reduction than aircraft overflights, so aircraft incidence geometry matters.

references.citation: Tang, S. K., Li, K. K. (2000). On the facade noise correction (PolyU). J. Acoust. Soc. Am.
references.supports_claim: Empirical 2.5-3 dB(A) facade corrections at 1 m are inadequate in most cases above absorbing ground.

references.citation: Okada, Y. et al. (2010). Scale model (1:40) of a street canyon with viaduct. Acoustical Science and Technology 31(1), 95.
references.supports_claim: Mean increase from multiple canyon reflections of up to about 8 dB (road traffic, indicative).

references.citation: Rizzi, S. A., Huff, D. L., et al. (2020). Urban Air Mobility Noise: Current Practice, Gaps, and Recommendations. NASA TP-2020-5007433.
references.supports_claim: NASA UAM Noise Working Group gap assessment, covering tools, testing and human response. A 2025 update exists (NTRS 20250011527). Its building-propagation content was not retrieved.

models.frequency_range_and_scale: Full audio band. Building to courtyard scale.
models.elevated_moving_source_suitability: These are direct measurements of elevated and overhead sources (S-76 rooftop, scale rotor approach, Schiphol overflights).

key_quantitative_findings: Reflection gain in the illuminated zone for an elevated eVTOL among building blocks: 0-5 dB above flat terrain (GBT; Yunus et al. 2023, AST 139:108410). Shadow-zone differences exceed 20-35 dB, but that model has no diffraction, so these are upper bounds.

Canonical image-source corner: about +8 dB vs free field. Canyon: +4 dB when source and receiver share a cross-section and up to +14 dB when 100 m apart along it, with the source 10 m high inside the canyon (Malbéqui, FA2023, doi:10.61782/fa.2023.0104). The spectra keep a single ground/wall interference dip in octave bands.

CNOSSOS-EU-based urban ray model vs NLR DigiCity measurements: very good agreement on reflection-dominated paths (160 Hz-6.3 kHz), but 10-15 dB underprediction on diffraction-dominated paths (Knepper et al., ERF 2025).

Overhead aircraft courtyard shielding (full-scale field lab near Schiphol): 9.5 dB(A) with line of sight vs 5.8 dB(A) without, distribution peaks at 13 and 5 dB(A), up to 14.6 dB(A) between exposed and shielded sides. Aircraft orientation explains R² = 0.58 of the variance (Wuite et al., FA2023). The 1:50 scale model reproduces in-situ relative levels to 0.5-4.2 dB(A) (Lugten et al., FA2023).

Helicopter approach to an elevated helipad (scale): ~60 dBA in front of the building vs ~25 dBA behind it. Facade interference swing ~20 dB at 5 cm from the wall, ~10 dB further away (Gibertini et al., Aerospace 2023, 10:701). Cited: Hilton and Pegg (NASA), at least 20 dB wall shielding for a police helicopter at 150 m.

Courtyards newly exposed to 100 m eVTOL routes: > 20 dB(A) rise in previously quiet semi-enclosed spaces. Urban attenuation frequency slope mostly < 1 dB/octave in band-averaged ray results (Feng and Kang, arXiv 2609.29763, CadnaA/ISO 9613).

Building-wake turbulence: received-level fluctuations > 3 dB at 100 Hz (Goyal et al., JASA 159:1304, 2026), comparable to the ~5 dB of source variability under gusts. LB-VLES reference cost ~2400 CPU-h per 1000 s of physical time (Goyal et al., JASA-EL 6:032801, 2026).

Costs: GBT vertiport footprint 55.7 s vs 3.7 s for a straight ray (15x), 122.5 s with wind, on 36 Xeon cores. GBT is 17x faster than FEM at 200 Hz. GBT surface truncation error goes from > 40 dB to < 8 dB with a semi-empirical correction (Yunus et al., JASA 153:2362, 2023). 3D ARD reaches ~450 Hz in minutes on a desktop and is about 100x faster than FDTD (Raghuvanshi et al., JASA 135:3231, 2014).

Facade microphones: the adjustment should be 6 dB flush-mounted and 3.5 dB near the facade (vs ASTM E966's 5 and 2). The loudspeaker method underestimates aircraft noise-level reduction by several dB (FAA DOT/FAA/TC-18/15). Simple 2.5-3 dB(A) facade corrections are inadequate over absorbing ground (Tang and Li, JASA 2000).

Multiple canyon reflections (road-traffic scale model): mean increase up to about 8 dB (Okada et al., AST 31:95, 2010). Sonic boom canyons: resonant modes prolong signals without raising loudness, and canyon-to-canyon variability is large when the aspect ratio is high (Dragna et al., JASA 2022, doi:10.1121/10.0010452).

Wave-based courtyard (PSTD, up to 500 Hz): a facade opening can raise courtyard levels by up to 10 dB(A) relative to over-roof paths, and 2D overpredicts distant-source contributions (Hornikx and Forssén 2011).
open_questions: Search budget ran out before I could cover several of the named groups: Pieren (Empa), Christian, Krishnamurthy and Greenwood (NASA/PSU), Hornikx on aircraft specifically, DLR, Gustave Eiffel, TU Berlin, Cambridge, Snellen and Simons (Delft drone measurements), Casalino's LBM community-noise work (AIAA 2019), Keith Wilson's 3D FDTD with buildings plus turbulence, and the Inter-Noise 2025 São Paulo CAA-plus-ray-tracing paper. None of these is cited above as verified. A follow-up pass should target them.
Full texts not retrieved: the Heli-STAR Vol. 5 S-76 rooftop dB results (DTIC blocked), Albert and Liu 2010 shadow-zone dB values, and Bian et al. 2021 building-case numbers.

I found no study that gives canyon gain or shielding as a systematic function of source elevation angle and canyon aspect ratio (H/W) for an elevated source well above the roofline. This is the key parameterisation for a NICEOPS reciprocity table and might be derived in-house from image-source plus edge diffraction.

Diffraction for steep overhead incidence is where models fail. NLR underpredicts by 10-15 dB and Yunus's GBT omits it. Which edge-diffraction formulation (UTD, Biot-Tolstoy-Medwin, Pierce wedge) holds for rotorcraft BPF harmonics (~10-100 Hz) diffracting into canyons is unresolved. Ray validity below a few hundred Hz is doubtful at canyon widths of 10-30 m.

Coherent vs incoherent summation: should interference in canyons be resolved per band, given turbulence (≥ 3 dB fluctuation) and moving-source Doppler? Octave and third-octave band averaging already flattens most of it (Malbéqui; Feng and Kang).

Validation data for an elevated, moving, full-scale rotorcraft over real canyons appear to be missing. The available sets are a drone at 8.5-20 m (NLR DigiCity), fixed-wing overflights (Schiphol field lab), scale models (Polimi, Delft), and the 1997 Heli-STAR rooftop data.

Inverse use: urban multipath (Wilson et al. 2006 coherence decay) and facade reflections (up to 20 dB spectral swing near walls) would bias de-propagated source spheres from microphones near structures. A facade/plate receiver correction or an exclusion criterion is needed.

verdict.family: Prior work on aircraft, rotorcraft, UAM and drone noise propagation in urban environments with buildings (aircraft_urban)

checked.item: Malbéqui (2023), FA2023 pp.1011-1014, doi:10.61782/fa.2023.0104: image-source corner and canyon cases vs Mithra (CSTB), 63 Hz-8 kHz octave bands, about +8 dB near the corner, canyon +4 dB in the same plane and +14 dB at 100 m apart with the source at z=10 m, ns=2(nr+1), Marignane 500 ft, ray theory invalid below a few tens of Hz, moving sources and buildings lower than the source left open
checked.correction: Full PDF read. The abstract says 'about 8 decibels', but the DAEL landing-page summary says 'about 9 dB'. Points the findings left out: the 'high-altitude' source is only z=30 m, and the ray-model buildings are 300 m tall, so every case puts the source below the roofline (the canyon walls are 300 m high, 30 m apart). That is the opposite of the NICEOPS case of a source above the roof. In the corner case the octave-band dip is at 1 kHz for the source 700 m away and at 250 Hz for the source 100 m away. The paper gives no timings.

checked.item: Knepper, Admiraal, Lammers (2025), ERF 2025, NLR DigiCity database: 22 microphones on 1.2 m tripods, 24 containers, M600 at 8.5 and 20 m, CNOSSOS-EU ray model with paths up to 3 levels deep, good agreement on reflection-only paths over 160 Hz-6.3 kHz, 10-15 dB underprediction on diffraction paths, background noise ruled out
checked.correction: Full PDF (ERF2025-518) read. Every number matches. The omni source played tones at 100, 200, 300 and 400 Hz plus broadband. Flight speeds were 1 and 10 m/s. The model uses 2D building outlines with heights (2.5D). A companion ERF2025 paper (Knepper, paper 009) reports that multirotor source models also underpredict, both tonal and broadband.

checked.item: Feng and Kang (2026), arXiv:2609.29763: CadnaA, ISO 9613, 3D buildings, ten 2x2 km districts, 100 m route, reflection loss 1 dB, search radius 2000 m, rises above 20 dB(A) in semi-enclosed spaces, attenuation slope mostly under 1 dB/octave
checked.correction: Full PDF read. Points the findings left out: routes are modelled as elevated LINE sources, time-averaged into Lden. The ground is G=0 (hard). The spectra are octave band. Absorption is fixed at 10 C and 70% RH. The authors also attribute the weak frequency slope partly to band-averaging of interference and partly to the ray method's poor low-frequency diffraction, which the findings did mention.

checked.item: Yunus, Casalino, Avallone, Ragni (2023), AST 139:108410: 0-5 dB reflection gain in illuminated zones, 20-35 dB shadow differences, BPF1 vs BPF2 up to 40 dB, wind over 30 dB in a single third-octave band, 55.7 s vs 3.7 s vs 46.6 s vs 122.5 s on a Xeon Gold 6140 (36 cores), 1.75 wavelengths, no diffraction
checked.correction: Full text read. Confirmed: urban vs flat terrain differs by 0-5 dB in illuminated zones, from multiple reflections. The timings and CPU are right. Directivity changes the footprint by up to 40 dB. Building size was set at 1.75x the first-BPF wavelength. Diffraction behind buildings is omitted. Corrections: (1) The '20-35 dB' shadow figure merges two different comparisons. Urban vs flat is 'more than 20 dB' in shadow zones. GBT vs straight rays is 'exceeds 35 dB' in terrain shadow zones. (2) The 'over 30 dB in a single 1/3-octave band' wind effect is NOT this paper's result. The paper quotes it from a prior road-traffic study across urban canyons (its ref 27). The paper itself also says the wind effect would be under 23 dB once diffraction and turbulence are included.

overstated_or_wrong_claims: Yunus et al. AST 2023: the over-30 dB single-third-octave wind effect is attributed to this paper. The paper is quoting a prior road-traffic urban-canyon study (its ref 27), and itself says the realistic wind effect would be under 23 dB once diffraction and turbulence are included.

Yunus et al. AST 2023: '20-35 dB shadow-zone differences' merges two comparisons. Urban vs flat is over 20 dB. GBT vs straight rays is over 35 dB in terrain shadows. Neither is physical, because diffraction is omitted.

The niceops_fit for the empirical-data model lists '20-35 dB shielding behind a building at high frequency' as a magnitude an urban module must reproduce. That number comes from a no-diffraction GBT model and should not be used as a validation target.

Malbéqui is described as including a 'source at high altitude' relevant to helicopters. Every case has the source at z = 10-30 m below 300 m-tall walls, so the canyon results (+4/+14 dB, channelling out of the open ends) concern a source inside the canyon. They do not transfer to a receiver in a canyon under a source well above the roofs.

The Tang and Li (2000, JASA) citation is wrong. The URL is S.-H. Tang's 2003 PolyU M.Phil. thesis, and it says the 2.5-3 dB correction is doubtful only for near-facade sources or receivers higher than 4 m, not 'inadequate in most cases'.
Mehra et al. 2014 (ARD) '~100x faster than FDTD' is not in the abstract and is unverified. The first author is Mehra, not Raghuvanshi.

The statistical fading model (Wilson et al. 2006) rests only on a 3-page meeting abstract. The substantive statements about frequency-independent exponential extinction should be sourced from later full papers.

Goyal JASA-EL quantitative details (decorrelation 1-2 s, ~2400 CPU-h, correlation coefficients, ~5 dB source variability) and the Gibertini dBA values could not be confirmed. Treat them as unverified.

The niceops_fit statement that 'band-averaged incoherent image sums ... are adequate above ~250 Hz' is the reviewer agent's own inference. Neither Malbéqui nor Feng and Kang demonstrates it; Malbéqui's octave bands still show a deep coherent dip at 250 Hz-1 kHz.
The claim that GBT is 'validated around 100-200 Hz with three building blocks' is plausible but was taken from the JASA abstract and not confirmed in the full text.
important_omissions: Canonical street-canyon theory: Lyon (1974) and Kang (2000, JASA 107, 'Sound propagation in street canyons: comparison between diffusely and geometrically reflecting boundaries'; 2002 radiosity papers). The diffuse vs specular facade reflection question is central to whether an image lattice is valid. Kang is cited for CadnaA but not for this.
The diffusion-equation and radiosity canyon models (Picaut, Valeau, Hornikx). Cheap energy-based canyon and courtyard models suit tabulation, and the Okada paper that was cited is itself one.

Facade scattering and diffuse-reflection coefficients (Ögren and Kropp; Van Renterghem, Hornikx and Forssén, 'The potential of building envelope greening...'; Hornikx and Forssén on facade irregularity). These limit coherent image sums.

Van Renterghem and Botteldooren's coupled PE-FDTD hybrids for canyon-to-canyon propagation, and the HOSANNA and QSIDE quiet-side projects. These are the main European urban-propagation groups and are not listed.
Pelat's modal approach to open urban waveguides (Pelat, Félix, Pagneux), which Malbéqui himself cites as ref [1]. It is a semi-analytic canyon transfer function suited to per-receiver tables.

Edge-diffraction formulations needed to fix the NLR 10-15 dB failure: Biot-Tolstoy-Medwin and the Svensson et al. (1999) secondary-source edge diffraction, Pierce (1974) wedge, Kouyoumjian-Pathak UTD, and Hadden-Pierce. They are named only in the open questions, with no references.

Better engineering methods than CNOSSOS for diffraction: Nord2000 and Harmonoise/IMAGINE (multiple-wedge Deygout-type diffraction, meteorological classes), plus documented CNOSSOS multiple-diffraction defects.

Precomputed and reciprocal wave-field approaches from room and game acoustics: Raghuvanshi and Snyder (2014, 'Parametric wave field coding for precomputed sound propagation', SIGGRAPH) and Microsoft Project Triton, plus equivalent-source and acoustic-transfer methods. These are the closest prior art to the roadmap's 'per-receiver urban reciprocity tables'.

Moving-source, time-domain urban methods: Doppler-aware image-source and time-variant ray methods for flyover auralization (Arntzen, NLR/TU Delft flyover auralization; Rizzi and Sahai NASA auralization with ground reflection; Pieren et al., Empa sonAIR/flyover auralization). The findings handle motion only quasi-statically.

Casalino et al. (AIAA SciTech 2019) 'Community noise of urban air transportation vehicles' (LBM with buildings). The findings name it in the open questions but do not review it, although it is the original Delft/Dassault urban UAM wave-based reference.

NASA RVLT and UAM urban acoustics work (for example NASA's UAM urban propagation and ambient-masking studies by Rizzi, Christian and Krishnamurthy), and the 2025 update of the UAM Noise Working Group TP (NTRS 20250011527), whose building-propagation content was not reviewed.

Building-shielding studies for fixed-wing aircraft beyond the TU Delft field lab, for example Flores et al. and the Gustave Eiffel / CSTB studies of quiet facades under flight paths, and DLR studies. Also reflections at elevated helipads beyond Polimi, such as the ERF 2021 'Helicopter noise in urban flight' paper (mentioned but not reviewed).

Urban microclimate and refraction over rooftops: Van Renterghem and Botteldooren's work on wind effects across canyons. It is the source Yunus quotes for the over-30 dB band effect and is directly relevant to elevated-source paths over roofs.
BEM, and 2.5D BEM for long canyons (for example Duhamel, Jean). This is the classic wave-based reference for canyon cross-sections at mid frequencies, and cheaper than 3D FDTD.
